topics.title: War, satyagraha and the Rowlatt Act

learn.hook: A thin man in a simple dhoti returned from South Africa with an idea so powerful that an empire did not know how to fight it: the power of truth.
points: The First World War created hardship in India: defence spending rose, taxes and customs duties went up, income tax was introduced, prices doubled between 1913 and 1918, and villagers faced forced recruitment into the army.
Crop failures in 1918-19 and 1920-21 and an influenza epidemic added to the suffering; 12 to 13 million people died in the famines and the epidemic.
Mahatma Gandhi returned to India in January 1915. Satyagraha meant fighting injustice through the power of truth and non-violence, appealing to the conscience of the oppressor.

His early satyagrahas: Champaran in Bihar (1917) against the oppressive indigo plantation system, Kheda in Gujarat (1917) for relief from revenue after crop failure and plague, and the Ahmedabad cotton mill workers (1918).

The Rowlatt Act (1919) let the government detain political prisoners without trial for two years. Gandhi called for a nationwide satyagraha with a hartal on 6 April 1919. On 13 April 1919, General Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, and hundreds were killed.

example.q: Think it through: Why did the Rowlatt Act anger Indians so much?
steps: It was hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council even though all Indian members opposed it.
It allowed people to be detained without trial for up to two years.
That meant the government could jail political workers without proving anything in court.
So Indians saw it as an attack on basic civil rights, and protests spread across the country.
example.answer: It allowed detention without trial and was passed despite united Indian opposition, so it was seen as an attack on basic rights.

learn.reallife: Every year on 13 April, people visit the Jallianwala Bagh memorial in Amritsar to remember those who lost their lives there in 1919.

quiz.q: When did Mahatma Gandhi return to India from South Africa?
quiz.explain: Gandhi came back in January 1915 and soon began local satyagrahas.
quiz.mistake: Confuses his return with later movements

quiz.q: What is the main idea of satyagraha?
options: Fighting injustice through the power of truth and non-violence
quiz.explain: Satyagraha stresses the power of truth. The satyagrahi wins the battle through non-violence by appealing to the conscience of the oppressor.
quiz.mistake: Thinks satyagraha means any kind of protest, including violent ones

quiz.q: Gandhi's 1917 satyagraha in Champaran, Bihar, was against what?
quiz.explain: In Champaran he inspired peasants against the oppressive plantation system. The Ahmedabad satyagraha (1918) was for mill workers.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the three early satyagrahas

quiz.q: Why did peasants of Kheda district in Gujarat need help in 1917?
options: They were forced to grow indigo
Crop failure and a plague epidemic left them unable to pay land revenue
quiz.explain: Gandhi organised satyagraha to support Kheda peasants who demanded relaxation of revenue collection.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Kheda with Champaran's indigo issue

quiz.q: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed the government to detain political prisoners without trial for how many years?
quiz.explain: The Act allowed detention without trial for two years, which Indians saw as deeply unjust.
quiz.mistake: Remembers the Act but not its details

quiz.q: On which date did Gandhi call for a nationwide hartal against the Rowlatt Act?
quiz.explain: The hartal was on 6 April 1919. 13 April 1919 is Jallianwala Bagh, and 6 April 1930 is when Gandhi made salt at Dandi.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up dates that share the same day or month

quiz.q: Where did the Jallianwala Bagh incident take place?
quiz.explain: Jallianwala Bagh is in Amritsar, Punjab. On 13 April 1919 troops under General Dyer fired on the gathered crowd.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the place with other places of the national movement

quiz.q: Which of these was a hardship caused in India by the First World War?
options: Forced recruitment into the army was banned
quiz.explain: War spending raised taxes and duties, introduced income tax and pushed prices up, while villages faced forced recruitment.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the actual effects of the war

teach.ask: Gappu asks softly: 'What was satyagraha, and why were people so upset in 1919?'
teach.praise: Thank you! Truth and non-violence against unjust laws. I understand now.
teach.nudge: What did the Rowlatt Act allow, and what happened at Jallianwala Bagh?

learn.hook: Gandhiji's idea was simple: British rule stands because Indians cooperate with it. Stop cooperating, and it will wobble!
points: In Hind Swaraj (1909) Gandhi argued that British rule in India survived only because of Indian cooperation. A Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919, and leaders such as the brothers Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali discussed united action with Gandhi.

At the Calcutta session (September 1920) Gandhi convinced leaders to start non-cooperation in support of Khilafat and swaraj; the programme was adopted at the Nagpur session in December 1920, and the movement began in January 1921.

The plan moved in stages: surrender of government titles, then boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods, and full civil disobedience if the government used repression.

In towns, students left government schools, teachers resigned, lawyers gave up their practice and foreign cloth was burnt. The value of imported foreign cloth fell from ₹102 crore to ₹57 crore between 1921 and 1922.

In Awadh, peasants led by Baba Ramchandra protested against talukdars and landlords; the Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up by October 1920. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, Alluri Sitarama Raju led a guerrilla struggle. Plantation workers in Assam left the estates, defying the Inland Emigration Act of 1859. Gandhi withdrew the movement in February 1922 after violence at Chauri Chaura.

example.q: Think it through: Why did the movement in the towns slow down after a while?
steps: Khadi cloth was often more expensive than mill cloth, so poor people could not afford it for long.
Boycotting British institutions needed Indian alternatives such as national schools and courts.
These alternatives came up slowly, so students and teachers began going back to government schools and lawyers to courts.
Without affordable substitutes, the boycott was hard to continue.
example.answer: Khadi was costly and Indian alternative institutions were slow to come up, so many people drifted back.

learn.reallife: When you see khadi kurtas on sale in a Khadi Gramodyog shop, remember that wearing khadi was once a bold act of protest.

games.title: True or false: Non-Cooperation
items: The Non-Cooperation programme was adopted at the Nagpur session of December 1920.
A compromise was worked out at Nagpur and the programme was adopted.
The Justice Party in Madras boycotted the council elections.
The Justice Party, a party of non-Brahmans, contested the elections as a way to gain power.
Gandhi withdrew the movement after the violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922.
He felt the movement was turning violent and satyagrahis needed more training.
Alluri Sitarama Raju's movement in the Gudem Hills was a guerrilla struggle.
It was a militant guerrilla movement, unlike Gandhi's non-violent methods.
Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, Assam plantation workers could leave the gardens whenever they wished.
The Act did not permit them to leave the tea gardens without permission.
Imports of foreign cloth rose sharply during 1921-22.
The value of foreign cloth imports fell from ₹102 crore to ₹57 crore.

quiz.q: In which book did Gandhi argue that British rule survived only because of Indian cooperation?
quiz.explain: Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in 1909. Anandamath is by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, Gulamgiri by Jyotiba Phule and Amar Jiban by Rashsundari Debi.
quiz.mistake: Confuses books from different parts of the syllabus

quiz.q: At which Congress session was the Non-Cooperation programme adopted?
quiz.explain: Gandhi convinced leaders at Calcutta in September 1920, and the programme was finally adopted at Nagpur in December 1920.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Lahore session that demanded Purna Swaraj

quiz.q: Which was one of the planned stages of the Non-Cooperation Movement?
options: Refusing to pay chaukidari tax in 1930
Surrender of titles awarded by the government
quiz.explain: The movement began with surrendering titles and moved to boycotts. Salt-making belonged to the Civil Disobedience Movement, and violence was against Gandhi's method.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Non-Cooperation with Civil Disobedience

quiz.q: Between 1921 and 1922, the value of imported foreign cloth fell from ₹102 crore to how many crore rupees?
quiz.explain: The boycott nearly halved foreign cloth imports, from ₹102 crore to ₹57 crore.
quiz.mistake: Does not remember the size of the fall

quiz.q: Who led the peasant movement in Awadh against talukdars and landlords?
quiz.explain: Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi who had earlier been an indentured labourer in Fiji, led the Awadh peasants. Alluri Sitarama Raju led the Gudem Hills struggle.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the peasant leader with the tribal leader

quiz.q: Alluri Sitarama Raju led a guerrilla movement in which region?
options: The Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh
quiz.explain: In the early 1920s Raju led tribal people of the Gudem Hills against restrictions on their forests.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the regions of different groups in the movement

quiz.q: Why did Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922?
options: He was elected to the legislative council
The British accepted all Congress demands
It was turning violent, as seen at Chauri Chaura
The Khilafat Committee asked him to
quiz.explain: After a clash at Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur turned violent, Gandhi felt satyagrahis needed proper training before mass struggles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the movement ended because it had won

quiz.q: Which leaders formed the Swaraj Party to return to council politics after the movement?
options: Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose
quiz.explain: C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party. Younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for radical mass agitation and full independence.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the founders of the Swaraj Party with younger radical leaders

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'How can you defeat an empire just by not cooperating? What did people actually do?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! If nobody cooperates, the system cannot run. Clever!
teach.nudge: What things did people boycott, and why did Gandhi stop the movement in 1922?

learn.hook: Salt! The cheapest thing in your kitchen became the spark that lit a nationwide movement.
points: The Simon Commission arrived in India in 1928 with no Indian member and was greeted with the slogan 'Go back Simon'. In October 1929 Viceroy Lord Irwin offered a vague 'dominion status' and a Round Table Conference.
In December 1929 the Lahore Congress, under Jawaharlal Nehru's presidency, formalised the demand for Purna Swaraj (complete independence), and 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day.

On 31 January 1930 Gandhi sent Lord Irwin a letter with eleven demands, including abolition of the salt tax, with a deadline of 11 March. He then marched with 78 volunteers over 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi in 24 days and broke the salt law on 6 April 1930.

People broke colonial laws: they made salt, picketed liquor shops, boycotted foreign cloth, refused to pay revenue and chaukidari tax, and violated forest laws. Rich peasants like the Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh, businessmen, industrial workers in the Nagpur region, and many women took part.

After the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931, Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in London in December 1931, but talks failed. Dr B.R. Ambedkar organised the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and sought separate electorates for dalits; the Poona Pact of September 1932 gave them reserved seats, voted for by the general electorate.

example.q: Think it through: Why did Gandhi choose salt as the symbol of the movement?
steps: Salt is used by everyone, rich and poor, in every home.
A tax on salt therefore hurt all Indians, especially the poor.
Making salt from sea water is simple and peaceful, so anyone could break the law non-violently.
So salt united people across classes against a clearly unfair British law.
example.answer: Salt was essential for everyone, so the salt tax was seen as the most oppressive face of British rule, and breaking it united all Indians.

learn.reallife: Next time you sprinkle namak on your sabzi, remember that a memorial at Dandi in Gujarat still honours the marchers of 1930.

quiz.q: Why was the Simon Commission opposed in India?
options: It did not have a single Indian member
It wanted to abolish the salt tax
quiz.explain: The Commission was to look into India's constitutional system, yet no Indian was on it, so it was met with 'Go back Simon'.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the main objection to the Commission

quiz.q: Which Congress session formalised the demand for Purna Swaraj?
quiz.explain: Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the Lahore session of December 1929, which demanded complete independence.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Lahore with Nagpur, or Jawaharlal with Motilal Nehru

quiz.q: Which day was celebrated as Independence Day after the Lahore session?
quiz.explain: 26 January 1930 was declared Independence Day; that is why our Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with 15 August, the day India actually became independent in 1947

quiz.q: How many volunteers marched with Gandhi from Sabarmati to Dandi?
quiz.explain: There were 78 volunteers. The march covered over 240 miles in 24 days, and Gandhi's letter had 11 demands.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the numbers linked with the Salt March

quiz.q: On which date did Gandhi break the salt law at Dandi?
quiz.explain: He reached Dandi and made salt by boiling sea water on 6 April 1930. 31 January was the letter, 11 March the deadline.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the date of the letter or deadline with the date of the act

quiz.q: How was the Civil Disobedience Movement different from the Non-Cooperation Movement?
options: It was limited only to the town of Dandi
People were asked not only to refuse cooperation but also to break colonial laws
It asked Indians to join the British army
quiz.explain: Non-Cooperation meant withdrawing cooperation; Civil Disobedience went further by deliberately breaking laws such as the salt law.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two movements were the same

quiz.q: Which business organisation was set up by Indian industrialists in 1927?
options: Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI)
quiz.explain: Industrialists like Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G.D. Birla formed FICCI in 1927 to protect Indian business interests.
quiz.mistake: Matches the wrong group with the organisation

quiz.q: What did the Poona Pact of September 1932 give the Depressed Classes?
options: Reserved seats in legislative councils, voted for by the general electorate
quiz.explain: Ambedkar had demanded separate electorates; Gandhi opposed this. The Poona Pact settled on reserved seats elected by the general electorate.
quiz.mistake: Confuses reserved seats with separate electorates

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'How did a pinch of salt shake the British Empire?'
teach.praise: Fantastic! A simple handful of salt became a symbol of freedom. Wah!
teach.nudge: What law did Gandhi break at Dandi, and how was this movement different from non-cooperation?

learn.hook: How do millions of people who speak different languages and eat different foods start feeling 'We are one'? Through songs, pictures, stories and flags!
points: Nationalism spreads when people feel they belong to one nation. This feeling grew through shared struggles and through culture: history, fiction, folklore, songs, popular prints and symbols.

The image of India as Bharat Mata was first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay. In the 1870s he wrote 'Vande Mataram' as a hymn to the motherland; it was later included in his novel Anandamath and was widely sung during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal.

Abanindranath Tagore painted a famous image of Bharat Mata as a calm, composed and spiritual figure. Nationalists also collected folk tales and songs; in Madras, Natesa Sastri published 'The Folklore of Southern India', a four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales.

During the Swadeshi movement in Bengal, a tricolour of red, green and yellow was designed, with eight lotuses for the eight provinces of British India and a crescent moon for Hindus and Muslims. By 1921 Gandhi had designed the Swaraj flag: red, green and white, with a spinning wheel in the centre.

Nationalists reinterpreted history to show India's achievements in art, architecture, science, mathematics, philosophy, crafts and trade in ancient times. They argued that colonial writers had wrongly called Indians backward.

example.q: Think it through: Why did nationalists put a spinning wheel at the centre of the Swaraj flag?
steps: The spinning wheel (charkha) stood for self-help and making our own khadi cloth.
Using khadi meant rejecting foreign, machine-made cloth.
Carrying the flag in marches showed defiance of British rule.
So the charkha turned an everyday tool into a symbol of swadeshi and self-reliance.
example.answer: The spinning wheel symbolised the Gandhian ideal of self-help and swadeshi, so the flag carried that message wherever it went.

learn.reallife: The Ashoka Chakra on today's Tiranga replaced the charkha of the Swaraj flag, but the idea of a flag that unites everyone continues.

games.title: Who made it?
pairs: Eight lotuses and a crescent moon

games.title: True or false: symbols of the nation
items: 'Vande Mataram' was later included in the novel Anandamath.
Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote the hymn in the 1870s and later included it in Anandamath.
The Swadeshi flag of Bengal had a spinning wheel at its centre.
The Swadeshi flag had eight lotuses and a crescent moon; the spinning wheel was on Gandhi's Swaraj flag of 1921.
The Swaraj flag of 1921 was red, green and white.
Gandhi's Swaraj flag used these three colours with a spinning wheel.
Natesa Sastri's collection was of Bengali folk tales.
He published a four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales.
Nationalists wrote about India's past achievements to counter the claim that Indians were backward.
Reinterpreting history was a way to build pride and confidence.

quiz.q: Who first created the image of Bharat Mata as an identity of India?
quiz.explain: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay created the image and wrote 'Vande Mataram' in the 1870s.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the creator of the image with Abanindranath Tagore's painting or other cultural figures

quiz.q: 'Vande Mataram' was later included in which novel?
quiz.explain: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay included the hymn in his novel Anandamath. It was widely sung in the Swadeshi movement in Bengal.
quiz.mistake: Picks another famous book from the syllabus

quiz.q: How did Abanindranath Tagore portray Bharat Mata in his painting?
options: As a calm, composed, spiritual figure
As a warrior queen riding a tiger
quiz.explain: His Bharat Mata is an ascetic figure who is calm and divine, giving food, clothing, learning and spiritual wisdom.
quiz.mistake: Mixes this painting with later, different images of Bharat Mata

quiz.q: What did Natesa Sastri publish?
options: A Hindi translation of the Ramcharitmanas
A four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales
quiz.explain: His 'The Folklore of Southern India' saw folklore as national literature reflecting people's real thoughts.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect Natesa Sastri with folklore

quiz.q: On the Swadeshi movement flag of Bengal, what did the eight lotuses stand for?
options: The eight provinces of British India
Eight demands made to the Viceroy
quiz.explain: The eight lotuses stood for the eight provinces, and the crescent moon represented Hindus and Muslims.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a meaning instead of recalling it

quiz.q: What was at the centre of the Swaraj flag designed by Gandhi by 1921?
quiz.explain: The Swaraj flag had a spinning wheel, symbolising self-help. The Ashoka Chakra is on today's national flag.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Swaraj flag with the present national flag or the Swadeshi flag

quiz.q: What were the colours of Gandhi's Swaraj flag of 1921?
quiz.explain: The Swaraj flag was red, green and white. Red, green and yellow was the Swadeshi flag of Bengal; saffron, white and green is today's Tiranga.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the colours of different flags

quiz.q: Why did Indian nationalists write about India's achievements in ancient times?
options: To ask the British to write India's history
To show that India had no past
To stop people from joining the national movement
To counter the colonial view that Indians were backward and to build pride
quiz.explain: By recalling achievements in art, science, mathematics, philosophy and trade, they encouraged people to take pride in the past and struggle against British rule.
quiz.mistake: Misses the purpose of reinterpreting history

teach.ask: Gappu sings: 'How can a song, a picture or a flag make people feel they belong to one nation?'
teach.praise: Beautiful! Songs, stories, pictures and flags tied people's hearts together.
teach.nudge: Can you name a song, an image and a flag that helped people feel Indian?
